title: AI and Reading Comprehension Part 2
author: Shanahan, Timothy
summary: In the second part of his series on AI and reading comprehension, Timothy Shanahan pivots from critique to construction: having argued in Part 1 that AI use which bypasses students' cognitive engagement guarantees non-learning, he now identifies a specific and legitimate role for AI in supporting teachers who work with complex texts. The central problem Shanahan addresses is practical: teachers regularly ask how to identify which sentences in a complex text will most confuse young readers, and existing guidance (look for long sentences, passive voice, multiple clauses) leaves teachers uncertain and under-confident. Shanahan proposes that AI is well-suited to this diagnostic task -- it can analyse a text and identify its five most complex sentences quickly, and with good enough reliability that teachers can make informed decisions about which text features to address with which students. The article illustrates this with ChatGPT applied to Kipling's 'How the Camel Got His Hump,' demonstrating plausible sentence-level complexity identification. Shanahan's larger argument is that AI should help teachers guide students through the challenges of complex text -- not help students evade those challenges. The proper use is analytic support for the teacher's instructional decision-making, not a tool for reducing text difficulty on students' behalf.
points: AI's legitimate instructional role is as a text analyst for teachers, not a simplifier for students -- it should help teachers decide which text features to explicitly address in instruction, not restructure the text to remove the challenge.

Question-type instruction (how to answer inferential questions, how to identify the main idea) has consistently failed to explain variance in reading achievement; what predicts comprehension is the complexity of the text itself and students' ability to navigate its specific features.

Shanahan's analogy is sharp: just as mom completing Janey's homework guarantees that Janey learns nothing, AI completing a student's reading task guarantees the student does not develop as a reader -- the learning is in the doing.

Comprehension instruction should address world knowledge, vocabulary, syntax, cohesion, discourse structure, literary devices, data presentation, and genre -- these are the text features students must learn to negotiate, not simplify away.

Teachers asking 'which sentences might confuse students?' currently get vague heuristics; AI can give them a specific, actionable shortlist, making the preparation for text-focused instruction faster and more precise.
quotes: Nobody can learn for you. We all must do our own learning. When students read a text and summarize it, they may or may not learn something. But when AI does this summarizing, a lack of learning is guaranteed.

Even when students seemingly do the work, AI may manage to prevent learning. Reading comprehension instruction tends to focus too much on how to answer certain kinds of questions and not enough on how to understand text.

That's why the use of AI to revise texts to facilitate comprehension is such a bad idea. The ability of AI to reliably transform a fifth-grade text into a third grade one without losing or damaging content has not yet been proven.
Such alterations reduce the possibility that the reading will contribute to improved comprehension. Altering the readability of a text -- when done well -- may ease reading comprehension.

I've decided that a better answer is to use artificial intelligence. Teachers don't have the time to do a thorough analysis of these kinds of text features, and AI can do a reasonably good job of identifying them.
Instead of helping kids to evade and avoid those challenges, it should help teachers to guide kids to deal with them.
